figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: The cost of long context. Dollar cost of generating $1$M output tokens on an existing input KV cache as a function of the context window size, obtained by converting the measured peak decode throughput of each deployment at on-demand H100 prices ($\$3.85$ per GPU-hour, Nebius, Sept. 2026). Input request lengths are drawn uniformly at random. GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.6 are served with INT4 weights and BF16 activations, Qwen 3 Coder Next is served in BF16. Serving at a context window size of $256$K rather than $16$K costs $3.6\times$ more per generated token for GLM, $5.6\times$ more for Kimi, and $7\times$ more for Qwen.
figures.headline: Cloud cost per generated token rises 3.6x to 7x when the serving context window grows from 16K to 256K across three open-weight models.
citing_sentences: Figure 1 shows the cloud token generation cost as a function of context window size for a selection of popular open-weight models.
First, the cloud-throughput study in Figure 1 uses models large enough to require multi-GPU deployment and exposes the effect of context window size under saturated serving load:
The cost values in Figure 1 convert these throughput measurements to the cost of $1$M output tokens using the stated hourly GPU price.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: The burden of long context. The token generation latency, token throughput, and memory footprint of several open-source models measured on an NVIDIA DGX Spark plotted as a function of input context length. For several models, later tokens take approximately 2x longer to generate than earlier tokens and require a larger memory footprint.
figures.headline: For several local models, later tokens take approximately 2x longer to generate and need a larger memory footprint.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 shows the token generation latency, throughput, and memory footprint of several popular locally-run coding models as a function of the input context length.
Second, we use locally deployable open-weight models for the on-device systems measurements in Figure 2 and for complementary task-level experiments.
The batch-one decode throughput in Figure 2 is the reciprocal of the mean inter-token latency.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Context-management regimes. The three context-management regimes considered in this work: Full-History Accumulation (FHA), End-of-Conversation Compaction (EoCC), and Single-Action Compaction (SAC).
figures.headline: Full-history, end-of-conversation and single-action compaction regimes differ in how much interaction history each step keeps.
citing_sentences: The regimes’ functioning is illustrated in Figure 3.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Decode throughput collapses as the context window size grows. Peak sustained decode throughput (tokens/s, left axis) for open-weight coding models served under vLLM on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, as a function of the configured context window size. GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.6 are served with INT4 experts and BF16 activations (Kimi additionally with an FP8 KV cache), Qwen 3 Coder Next in BF16. The right axis re-expresses the same curve as a speedup over the $256$K operating point. Reducing the context window size from $256$K to $16$K buys $3.6\times$ (GLM 5.2), $5.6\times$ (Kimi K2.6), and $7\times$ (Qwen 3 Coder Next) more decoded tokens per second on identical hardware.
figures.headline: Decode throughput falls as context window grows, so shrinking from 256K to 16K gives 3.6x to 7x more tokens per second.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Long-horizon results as a function of total context limit. Top: accuracy changes in percentage points relative to each model’s full-history baseline; zero indicates unchanged accuracy. Bottom: baseline estimated optimized retail cost divided by the compaction configuration’s estimated optimized retail cost; $1\times$ indicates unchanged cost. Orange/blue identify Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol, respectively, and stars mark the baselines. Cost estimates use the model in Appendix B.
figures.headline: Long-horizon accuracy stays within a few points of baseline for both models as the total context limit shrinks.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 plots the EoCC accuracies and estimated cost savings relative to FHA baselines against increasing levels of compaction.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Long-input results as a function of total context limit. Top: accuracy changes relative to each model’s full-input baseline. Bottom: optimized retail cost savings, using the model in Appendix B.
figures.headline: Long-input accuracy remains near or above full-input baselines for both models across the tested total context limits.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 plots the EoCC accuracies and estimated cost savings relative to FHA baselines against one or multiple levels of compaction.

figures.caption: LongBench v2: conversation length versus document length. Claude Opus 4.5, compaction at $16$K / $12$K. The document-length axis is logarithmic and the conversation-length axis is linear. The dashed curve marks $y=x$.

abstract: Abstract. Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens. On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x. Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.

sections.body: Token generation latency and memory grow with context length, so later tokens cost more to generate. Figure 1 converts measured peak decode throughput into USD cost per 1M output tokens for three open-weight models, and the text reports cost reductions of 3.6x to 7x. Figure 2 measures local inter-token latency on a DGX Spark, where it approximately doubles for several models across the measured context lengths. Table 1 shows that context windows of 200K to 1.05M tokens exceed the length of many literary works. The paper asks three research questions: whether long-horizon tasks and long-input tasks can be completed without long contexts, and whether long-horizon tasks can be completed with one action per context.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Serving at 256K tokens costs 3.6x to 7x more per generated token than serving at 16K for open-weight models.

sections.body: The paper defines terms such as context, context window size, long-horizon task and long-input task. It compares three regimes: full-history accumulation (FHA), which appends every action and observation; end-of-conversation compaction (EoCC), which writes a bounded, task-relevant compaction of the state when a threshold is crossed; and single-action compaction (SAC), which runs one environment action per fresh conversation with a compact semantic state. Long-horizon benchmarks include SWE-bench Verified with 500 instances and FRAMES with 824 questions. Long-input benchmarks include LongBench v2 with 503 questions and BABILong with 550 evaluated questions. Long inputs are stored as files for selective reading with Bash tools. Principal accuracy runs use Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Three context regimes are compared on six long-horizon and seven long-input benchmarks with frontier and open-weight models.

sections.body: EoCC runs on six long-horizon benchmarks at total context limits from 48K/36K down to 8K/6K, depending on the benchmark. Across all configurations, Claude Opus 4.5 ranges from -3.7 to +5.6 percentage points relative to its full-history baseline, and GPT 5.6 Sol ranges from -3.3 to +4.4. No more than 5 of 22 threshold configurations per model lose more than 2 percentage points. Estimated cost savings range from 2.2x to 8.8x for Opus 4.5 and from 2.4x to 5.0x for GPT 5.6 Sol. The paper states that compaction is lossy and gives a coin-toss example in which a fixed budget eventually loses required records. Its conclusion is that the full history need not stay in context, not that history is unnecessary.
sections.heading: Long-horizon tasks don’t need long contexts
sections.headline: Compacting context keeps long-horizon accuracy between -3.7 and +5.6 percentage points of baseline for Claude Opus 4.5.

sections.body: Seven long-input benchmarks are run with selective input reading, in which the agent reads stored documents with Bash tools, and compaction is available as a fallback. Compared with full-input baselines, Claude Opus 4.5 ranges from -0.4 to +40.0 percentage points and GPT 5.6 Sol from +1.0 to +30.9. Estimated cost savings are 6.5x to 54.6x for Opus 4.5 and 4.4x to 233.3x for GPT 5.6 Sol, combining selective reading with shorter windows. Figures 7 and 8 plot summed conversation length against document length on LongBench v2 and LOONG. Conversation lengths stay in broadly similar bands as documents grow. The paper reports one benchmark that stays close to baseline rather than above it.
sections.heading: Long-input tasks don’t need long contexts
sections.headline: Selective reading of input files with compaction as fallback matches or beats full-input baselines on almost all long-input benchmarks.

sections.body: Single-action compaction runs each action in a fresh conversation that holds only the task and a compact semantic state. For Claude Opus 4.5 it preserves the mini-swe-agent baseline on SWE-bench Verified and improves Terminal-Bench by 4.6 percentage points. For GPT 5.6 Sol it reaches 82.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 84.3% on Terminal-Bench, which is below its baseline by 2.0 and 3.3 percentage points. Median peak live context is 7–9K tokens across both models and benchmarks, and the maximum falls from 130–200K to 15–37K tokens. The paper describes GPT 5.6 Sol's reductions as small and proposes semantic state space models (SSSMs) as a model class built around this kind of state.
sections.heading: Compaction can be performed after every action
sections.headline: Single-action compaction preserves or improves Claude Opus 4.5 accuracy, while GPT 5.6 Sol drops 2.0 and 3.3 points.

sections.body: The paper answers yes to its three research questions: long-horizon tasks, long-input tasks, and long-horizon tasks with one action per context can be completed without long contexts in the settings tested. The authors conclude that long contexts are not necessary for the long-context tasks studied. They also state that the evidence does not rule out tasks where long context helps, and does not prove that every task can be solved in short context. The paper argues that post-training changes could shrink context window sizes, which would lower cloud token cost and speed up local inference.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Long contexts were not necessary in the tested settings, though the evidence does not rule out tasks that need them.

sections.body: Appendix A describes compaction contents that preserve accuracy: a near-verbatim copy of the task, the agent's current plan, and artifacts relevant to future work. Appendix B gives the cost estimation formula, a rounded mean cost ratio of 0.20, a 5:1 output-to-uncached-input price ratio, and reference prices of USD 25 for Opus 4.5 and USD 20 for GPT 5.6 Sol. Appendix C reports per-benchmark tables for SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, Terminal-Bench, FRAMES, and BFCLv3. Appendix D shows open-weight results, where Qwen 3 Coder Next falls from 53.0% to 3.6% on SWE-bench Verified at 16K / 12K. Appendix E gives selective reading examples, Appendix F gives long-input tables, and Appendix G gives compaction prompt outlines.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix covers compaction design, cost estimation, detailed per-benchmark results, open-weight models, and agent prompt outlines.
